title: Project on childhood obesity
titleCn: 儿童肥胖研究项目讨论

paragraphs.text: Part three.
You will hear a sociology student called Richard discussing his research project with his tutor.
First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
Hi, Professor Kerrigan.
Oh, hi, Richard. Come in. You wanted to see me about your research project?
That's right.
Okay. Now, uh, remind me what it's about.
Uh, childhood obesity.
Okay. And what aspect in particular?

Well, there's lots out there about adults and the effect that being overweight has on their health. But I wanted to concentrate on children. Mainly, I want to understand the factors that underlie the rise in obesity levels among this group of the population.
Hmm, right. So you said you were having some trouble with the project?
Yes. I've done the background reading, but I'm a bit lost as to how to get started on the actual research. I know I'll need quite a lot of data, but I just keep going round in circles.
Hmm, I see.
Well, one thing you'll presumably be focusing on is diet.
Mm, actually, I think the relationship between obesity and exercise is more interesting.
Hmm.

From what I've read, it seems people are still very uncertain about the relationship between body weight and physical activity. So I suppose that's what I'd like to look at, even though diet might be simpler to research.
Do you think children are getting less exercise?
Mm, yes. Maybe it's the safety issue. In this society, parents are much more concerned about their children walking around by themselves nowadays than they were a generation ago.
Why do you think that is?
Uh, I suppose that there's more crime nowadays.
But have you checked to see whether that's actually the case?
Uh, no.
And if you do, I think you'll find that's not what's going on. Statistically speaking, many types of crime in the UK haven't increased much, but what crime there is gets a lot more media coverage.
Mm, right. So parents don't let their kids go out walking on their own.
Mm, exactly. So why else might children be getting less exercise?
Well, a lot more people in the UK actually have a car nowadays than thirty years ago.
And if we look to the future, what does this increase in vehicle ownership suggest?
Uh, poorer air quality?
Yes, but that's not related to your topic.
Mm. Well, I suppose it could mean that these children will grow into adults who think they're unable to get by without a car.
Right.
Uh, some kids now, uh, they moan if their parents park at the far side of the supermarket car park. They can't be bothered to walk even that far.
Mm. So have you done any reading in this specific area?
Well, I did find some figures about the increase in the numbers of children being driven to school.
As compared with those walking to school?

Right. Uh, it's huge. I mean, parents drive their children to school because they're afraid of them being involved in road accidents. But then that means that often the family needs a second car, so there's more traffic.
And the roads near the school are really congested at certain times of the day. It's ironic, isn't it?
Right. So I could look at that, seeing if there's any link between obesity and whether children walk to school or are driven there.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
Okay, so you're looking at the relationship between obesity and children walking to school.
Mm.
What criteria could you use to select the children for your research?

Well, I could ask children from the local school. I know some children there travel quite a long distance to school, and others are quite close. I'd need to decide on the ages. Uh, maybe I'd just look at two groups of different ages.
Mm. You might find you have too many variables. I'd limit it to the same age range.
All right. And I suppose I should have fifty percent boys and fifty percent girls?
Well, I wouldn't worry if it's not possible. You do need quite a range of children, though, as far as their physical build is concerned.
Oh, how tall they are and how much they weigh?
Mm-hmm.
Okay. It'd be interesting to know about their attitudes to exercise too.
That'd be something that comes up in your research later on, I think.
Okay.
So have you any idea what you expect to find out?
Uh, well, one thing is whether children who walk to school are more likely to be involved in accidents than those who drive.
Mm-hmm.
Hmm. I don't think they will be. And it'll be interesting to see if they have the same levels of activity as the other children during the day.
Hmm. Do you expect them to?

Uh, I don't know. I think they're more likely to get more exercise generally, you know, to do more sport outside school even. And I'd expect a positive relationship between walking to school and not being obese. But as far as academic performance goes, well, I don't expect to see any correlation there, but you never know.
Hmm. Right. Well, I...
That is the end of part three. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part three.
